section.sectionSummaryBrief: The verse continues to explain the details of divine service in order from the light to the heavy, beginning with the acquisition of a Hebrew slave, which includes two aspects: the Canaanite slave and the Hebrew slave.
section.t: And the verse continues to explain the details of the service, and in order from the light to the heavy,
for the service must be in a manner of "little by little I will drive them out."
And the beginning of the service is in what is written,
"When you acquire a Hebrew slave," etc.,
for in this are included two aspects in service,
the aspect of a Canaanite slave and the aspect of a Hebrew slave,
as understood from what is stated in the Mechilta
and brought in Rashi's commentary on the Torah
(from which it is understood that this is also according to the simple meaning of the verse),
that "a Hebrew slave" means a slave who is a Hebrew, or perhaps it means the slave of a Hebrew
(a Canaanite slave that you purchased from a Jew),
the verse teaches, etc.,
for the conclusion is that it refers to a slave who is a Hebrew,
but nevertheless there is a possibility to think
(also in the simple meaning of the verse as above)
that it is a Canaanite slave, and a special teaching is needed
(the verse teaches)
to negate this reasoning,
from which it is understood that there is room to say
(as a possibility to think)
that it also refers to a Canaanite slave.
And in this
(in the aspect of a Canaanite slave)
is the beginning of the service,
and afterwards he elevates in his service and reaches the aspect of a Hebrew slave,
until he reaches the aspect of a Hebrew maidservant,
and as will be explained below.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: There are three levels in the soul—Canaanite slave, Hebrew slave, and Hebrew maidservant—corresponding to Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, which are the levels of the wicked, the intermediate, and the righteous, and the order of service progresses from the lowest to the highest.
section.t: And the explanation is,
as explained in the discourses
at length
[and particularly in the discourse about which the Tzemach Tzedek writes in Ohr HaTorah

that this discourse is from our great master, may his soul be at rest, etc., and it is a very esteemed discourse, etc., and it is about the levels of the righteous, the wicked, and the intermediate mentioned in the Tanya],
that there are three levels in the soul of man,
Canaanite slave,
Hebrew slave, and Hebrew maidservant,
and their meaning is the three levels of Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah,
and it is explained there that they are the matter of the righteous, the wicked, and the intermediate.
And in this is the order of service: first is the service of the aspect of a Canaanite slave, and afterwards a Hebrew slave and a Hebrew maidservant,
as it is stated in the Zohar in Saba DeMishpatim,
"When a person is born, they give him a Nefesh... if he merits more, they give him a Ruach... if he merits more, they give him a Neshamah,"
for immediately at the time of birth, the aspect of Nefesh is drawn to everyone
(among the levels of the soul),
that from this aspect, the service is in the aspect of Nefesh,
and afterwards, through his service, he ascends to the aspect of Ruach, which is more elevated,
until he reaches the aspect of Neshamah
(and to the service that comes from these aspects),
as explained in the details of the differences in the service of Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah in Kuntres HaAvodah.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: The aspect of a Canaanite slave applies to both the wicked and the intermediate, because even though the intermediate has an external desire for license, his inner essence is a part of G-d above, which will ultimately be actualized, making him a true intermediate.
section.t: And behold, in the explanation of the matter of a Canaanite slave, there is a discussion in the glosses and notes and explanations of the Tzemach Tzedek in Ohr HaTorah
whether this is the aspect of a wicked person who has it good, or the intermediate mentioned in the Tanya,
and he concludes there
that both are true.
Accordingly,
the aspect of a Canaanite slave refers to both the wicked and the intermediate.
And at first glance, it requires explanation,
for how is it possible that one who is in the aspect of a slave,
"a slave prefers to be licentious"
[that his main desire and satisfaction is in licentiousness... and he goes after the stubbornness of his heart,
and what he does and serves is only against his will, due to fear of judgment, lest he be struck with a rod,
as explained at length in the discourses],
could be in the aspect of an intermediate
[and fulfill the oath to be an intermediate],
for the intermediate has never committed a transgression and will never commit one, as explained in the Tanya,
and as is known the saying of the early Chassidim, "If only I were an intermediate."
But the explanation is,
that being an intermediate is within the capacity of every person
(including this one who "prefers to be licentious")
as understood from the fact that in the title "Book of Intermediates"
(which is the subject of the book)
the Alter Rebbe writes
[and it is known
that even the title was written by the Alter Rebbe]
"For the matter is very near to you"
"in your mouth and in your heart to do it,"
and in the body of the Tanya
he further writes that the trait of the intermediate is the trait of every person
[meaning that even from the perspective of measurement and limitation
(for the matter of measure
(trait)
can only be said when there is a defined measure of limitation)
behold, the aspect of the intermediate is according to the action and measure of each person,
for whoever it may be from Israel
(every person)
is included in "you are called 'man'"
referring to "likeness to the supernal."
And moreover
(as he continues in the Tanya there)
"and
afterwards every person
will draw"
[for in this
(in the word "will draw")
there are two interpretations—like in "and you shall love"
—a command and a promise for the future].
And the reason for this is,
for even this that "he prefers to be licentious"
(as above)
is only in externality,
but his inwardness—"the trait of every person and afterwards every person will draw"—is that he is literally a part of G-d above,
and as the well-known ruling of the Rambam,
that when they coerce him
(for he prefers otherwise)
and he says "I desire," this is his true desire
[for that he prefers to be licentious is not him, but his evil inclination compelled him],
and surely his inwardness
(his inwardness)
will come into actuality as above
("will draw" is future tense and a promise)
"in your mouth and in your heart to do it,"
in thought, speech, and deed,
including the fulfillment of the oath that they administer to him
(at least "do not be wicked"
(rather an intermediate))
as in the Tanya
[for this is also the interpretation of "and afterwards every person will draw,"
that the person
(from the perspective of his soul)
is drawn to be an intermediate,
which takes him out of whatever state and situation he may be in his service],
for surely
(even if he needs to repent)
his end is to repent, and as the promise
"for no outcast shall be cast out from Him"
[and on the contrary,
through repentance he will come to a more elevated level,
as the statement,
"In the place where penitents stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand"].
And until, from the perspective of his inwardness,
behold, he is always very near to this
(that it be "in your mouth and in your heart to do it,"
in thought, speech, and deed—like an intermediate)
very.
And based on this, it will also be understood in our matter, that even though a Canaanite slave "prefers to be licentious," nevertheless his level is the aspect of the intermediate,
for ultimately he will surely say "I desire"
(from the perspective of his inwardness)
for "no outcast shall be cast out," etc.
